nameStory: The name 'water pennywort' comes from the plant's distinctive round, coin-shaped leaves that look just like tiny green pennies floating on water. The scientific name 'batrachium' means 'of frogs' in Latin, hinting at this plant's love for the same wet places where frogs like to hang out!
description: **[UNCERTAIN SPECIES - EXTREMELY RARE]** This is a tiny aquatic or semi-aquatic plant that forms small mats in shallow water or muddy shores. It produces miniature round leaves, each about the size of a dime, that sit on delicate creeping stems. The entire plant stays very low and small, rarely growing more than a few inches tall, making it easy to overlook among other wetland vegetation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfect circles about dime-sized with smooth edges and visible radiating veins like spokes on a tiny wheel. Feel smooth and slightly succulent to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low creeping mats with stems that root at joints where they touch mud or shallow water. Stems feel soft and break easily when handled.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny inconspicuous white or greenish clusters that appear near the leaf bases. So small you might need a magnifying glass to see the individual flowers clearly.

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in or right at the water's edge - muddy pond shores, shallow pools, or areas that flood regularly. Never in dry soil.

habitat: **[UNCERTAIN]** Likely found along muddy shores of ponds, slow streams, and seasonal pools where water levels fluctuate. Prefers shallow areas with soft, muddy substrates where it can root easily. May also grow in permanently shallow water less than a few inches deep.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water warms, with fresh round leaves appearing on creeping stems. This is when the plant is most actively growing and spreading.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full mats of circular leaves. Tiny flowers appear during this time but are easily missed without close inspection.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows and some leaves may yellow or die back as temperatures drop. Seeds likely develop during this period.
seasonality.winter: **[UNCERTAIN]** May die back completely or persist with reduced foliage depending on water temperature and ice cover.

funFact: With only one recorded observation in all of New England, you're more likely to spot a rare bird than find this tiny plant - making any discovery a potential botanical treasure hunt victory!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other water pennyworts, especially American Water-pennywort, which has similar round leaves. **[UNCERTAIN]** The key differences may be in leaf size, stem characteristics, or precise habitat preferences, but with so few observations, field identification guides for this species are extremely limited.
contextualKnowledge: This species is so rare in New England that field identification information is extremely limited. Any suspected sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanists or natural heritage programs, as it could represent a significant botanical discovery.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN]** Compared to its more common cousin American Water-pennywort, this species likely differs in leaf size, flower arrangement, or specific habitat requirements. However, distinguishing between water pennywort species often requires expert knowledge and sometimes microscopic examination of flower parts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American water-pennywort can be distinguished from its relatives by its consistently round leaves and preference for the northeastern climate.
Among New England's water pennyworts, manyflower marshpennywort has the most perfectly circular leaves and the most obvious umbrella-shaped flower clusters.
Among New England's pennyworts, whorled pennywort is the easiest to identify because of its perfectly circular leaves attached at the center.
Unlike American Water-pennywort which has kidney-shaped or lobed leaves, Sibthorp's Pennywort has perfectly round, unlobed leaves.
Unlike its pennywort relatives in New England, floating marsh pennywort is the only one that forms true floating mats on open water.
